questions.prompt: What major capability does the `@Observable` macro introduce to SwiftUI?

options.text: It tracks property access so views only redraw when properties they read change.
options.explanation: Right. @Observable provides precise property-level observation for views.

options.text: It runs all view body calculations on background queues automatically.
options.explanation: View body calculations still execute on the main thread in SwiftUI.

options.text: It converts Swift classes into value types behind the scenes.
options.explanation: @Observable applies specifically to reference types and keeps them classes.

options.text: It forces every view in the app to redraw whenever any model property changes.
options.explanation: That was the old behavior of ObservableObject, which @Observable solves.

questions.prompt: Why does `@Observable` reduce view redraws compared to `ObservableObject`?

options.text: It tracks properties individually instead of invalidating on any change.
options.explanation: Right. Views only redraw if they read the specific property that changed.

options.text: It disables animation curves so that rendering is instantaneous.
options.explanation: Animations work normally with @Observable.

options.text: It limits SwiftUI views to a maximum of sixty updates per second.
options.explanation: Redraw reduction comes from precise dependency tracking, not a frame cap.

options.text: It skips drawing any view that is currently located offscreen.
options.explanation: View invalidation logic is independent of viewport visibility.

questions.prompt: Explain how `@Observable` improves SwiftUI rendering performance compared to the older `ObservableObject` protocol. Provide your answer in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: `@Observable` tracks property access at runtime on an individual property level. With `ObservableObject`, changing any `@Published` property caused every observing view to re-render. With `@Observable`, a view only redraws when a property it actually read inside its body changes. This prevents unnecessary view evaluations and makes the view hierarchy much faster.

rubric.criterion: Mentions that @Observable tracks changes at the individual property level rather than the whole object.
Contrasts with ObservableObject where changing any property re-renders all observing views.
Explains that avoiding unnecessary redraws improves view evaluation performance.

questions.prompt: How do you manage model ownership and passing in SwiftUI views when using `@Observable`? State which property wrappers to use for ownership, read-only passing, and two-way bindings in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: In the parent view that owns the model, declare it using `@State private var model = MyModel()`. To pass the model to a child view for read or action access, declare it as a plain property like `let model: MyModel`. If the child view needs two-way bindings to the model properties for input controls, annotate the property with `@Bindable var model: MyModel`.

rubric.criterion: Identifies @State as the property wrapper for owning an @Observable model in a view.
Explains that child views can accept the model as a regular property without wrappers.
Identifies @Bindable for creating two-way bindings in child views.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of `@ObservationIgnored` and when should you use it? Explain in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: `@ObservationIgnored` tells the Observation macro not to track changes for a specific stored property. You should use it for properties that do not affect the user interface, such as internal identifiers, temporary caches, or helper loggers. This prevents unnecessary observation overhead when those internal values change.

rubric.criterion: Explains that @ObservationIgnored opts a stored property out of change tracking.
Provides realistic examples like internal IDs, cache state, or non-UI metadata.

questions.prompt: How does passing an `@Observable` model through the environment differ from the older `@EnvironmentObject` pattern? Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: With `@Observable`, you inject the model using `.environment(model)` without needing an explicit key. In child views, you read the model using `@Environment(MyModel.self) var model`. This replaces `@EnvironmentObject` and eliminates the need for conformance to `ObservableObject`.

rubric.criterion: Explains that injection uses .environment(model) rather than .environmentObject(model).
Explains reading via @Environment(Type.self) rather than @EnvironmentObject.
Notes that conformance to ObservableObject is no longer required.

questions.prompt: Why can you not use `@StateObject` with an `@Observable` model class? Explain in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: `@StateObject` requires its wrapped value to conform to the `ObservableObject` protocol. The `@Observable` macro generates Swift Observation code rather than `ObservableObject` conformance. Attempting to pass an `@Observable` class to `@StateObject` results in a compile-time type mismatch error. Instead, use `@State` to own `@Observable` models.

rubric.criterion: States that @StateObject requires conformance to ObservableObject.
Explains that @Observable does not conform to ObservableObject, causing a compiler error.
Mentions using @State as the correct alternative for @Observable ownership.
